questions.question: Develop a business plan for one of the ideas mentioned below, also develop a business model highlighting the various components of the same. (20) + (10) a) Aha Design, Stroud, GREAT BRITAIN (ahadesign.co.uk) Aha Design’s aim is to fight youth unemployment by providing young people with paid opportunities to showcase their digital talents, get client recommendations and improve their employability in the digital sector. Many young people already have the necessary skills to get a job in this sector but lack the opportunities to prove themselves to employers so Aha Design tries to solve this problem. Any young person can sign up at www.ahadesign.co.uk and will be accepted if they are suitably skilled in one of the service areas including graphic design, web development, app development and video production. Aha currently has 50 students signed up and is continuing to grow. Its clients range from individuals and charities to businesses and government institutions. b) Carrot, Mexico City, MEXICO (carrot.mx/site) Carrot is Mexico's first car sharing service—an affordable and convenient alternative to the high costs and hassles of owning or renting a car. The startup offers cars of various sizes that are kept at self-service pods throughout the city. Customer can then use a vehicle by renting it (through their smartphone) by the hour or day and accessing it with an RFID card, with tariffs including gas and insurance. It has been proven that each shared vehicle removes between 15 and 20 private vehicles from circulating daily. Carrot's long term goal is to diminish up to 1% of Mexico City's car traffic and pollution (over 40,000 less vehicles circulating daily). (HUM-592) Page 1 of 3 c) E-LAB, Nairobi, Kenya E-Lab is a startup that aims at eradicating electronic waste in Nairobi, Kenya— a rather new environmental problem due to Africa's exponential growth of the number of mobile phone users and electronics over the last couple of years as well as to promote a culture of safe and responsible e-waste disposal among Kenyans. E-Lab transforms this hazardous e-waste into innovative products including art pieces and sculptures for the art industry, jewelry and shoes made from rubber and recycled plastic found in electronic devices for the fashion industry and “juakali” or metallic money boxes from copper and other metals. Alongside mopping up hazardous electronic waste for a cleaner and safer society, E-Lab would keep diseases like cancer in check and would also help curb unemployment which is a major socio-economic challenge in Africa. d) EnerKey, Ciudad Lopez Mateos, MEXICO EnerKey is dedicated to the technological development in processes for obtaining hydrogen as an alternative, pollution-free fuel. It has designed a device to reduce consumption and make the process feasible and affordable. e) Frilp.com ( Friends Help), Chennai, INDIA (frilp.com) Frilp—short for Friend's Help—is a platform to discover shopping, businesses and services through personalized recommendations from your friends and trusted circle. Inspired by the way trusted information gets passed over in real world, Frilp is built to counter information overload as well as the generalization and anonymity in the current ratings and reviews system for businesses. Frilp identifies the right people in your network who are most probable to help you with the recommendation you are looking for while surfacing relevant recommendations for you to consume instantly. f) Get In, Mexico City, MEXICO Get In uses facial recognition technology to identify consumers as they enter retail locations. Based on a predefined profile of their habits, preferences, and taste, Get In sends them the most relevant messages, advertisements and other information tailored to their profiles. g) KARIBU Solar Power, Dar es Salaam, TANZANIA (karibusolar.com) KARIBU Solar Power is an innovative enterprise that makes high quality solar lighting and mobile phone charging affordable. It produces a modular solar lamp: solar panel, rechargeable battery with mobile phone charger, and light - and employs an innovative business model that allows consumers to pay in small increments, just like they would for kerosene. This makes it affordable to the 500+ million Africans who do not have adequate access to light and energy—helping create a world where everyone has access to clean, safe and affordable light and energy. By providing Africa's most disadvantaged with affordable access to light and mobile phone charging, we are able to improve education and health, increase families’ savings and reduce carbon emissions. By leveraging micro-franchisees and local infrastructure, it creates new income for communities and provides superior lighting and mobile phone charging that is far more affordable than dangerous and environmentally damaging kerosene and alternatives. (HUM-592) Page 2 of 3 h) Panacea, Dhaka, BANGLADESH (www.panacealive.com) Panacea is a mobile application which lets customers verify by themselves whether a medicine is genuine or fake—an all-too-common problem in Bangladesh. The startup imprints a unique 8-digit-code, a QR code and a three-color code sequence into every medicine pack in its manufacturing line. During purchase, a customer enters the 8-digit-code or simply scans the QR code. If the information on the product packaging matches the information stored in the app, the medicine is genuine. If there is no match, the app automatically sends a notice of forgery including place, time and type of medicine forged to its servers for taking action against counterfeiters. i) Teddy the Guardian, Zagreb, CROATIA (teddytheguardian.com) Teddy The Guardian is an individually designed and completely organic plush teddy bear that measures children's vital signs seamlessly as they play—in a way that is completely intuitive and interactive causing no stress or inconvenience for the child.
